question: What is the best place to hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer?
body:
## Direct Answer

The best place to hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a specialized fractional-executive firm or vetted marketplace (such as Chief Outsiders, Bespoke Partners, Go Fractional, or Continuum) rather than a generic job board, because these channels pre-screen for the operator experience, revenue-model fit, and part-time engagement structure that a fractional CRO role demands. For most B2B companies between roughly two and fifty million in revenue, the fastest path to a strong hire is a warm referral from your investors or peer CEOs, backed up by a specialist firm that can present two or three qualified candidates inside two weeks.

Choosing where to source a fractional CRO matters more than most founders expect, because the "where" quietly determines the "who." A generalist recruiter surfaces a different candidate pool than a RevOps-focused marketplace, and a LinkedIn cold search surfaces yet another. The right channel depends on your stage, your budget, the specific gap you are filling, and how much hand-holding you need on scoping the role. Below we break down every credible sourcing channel, what each one costs in time and money, how to vet the candidates it produces, and how to structure the engagement so the person you hire actually moves revenue instead of just attending your pipeline meetings.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO and why does the sourcing channel matter?

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior go-to-market leader who owns the entire revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, partnerships, and often customer success — on a part-time, ongoing basis, typically one to three days a week. Unlike an interim CRO who parachutes in full-time to cover a gap, a fractional CRO is a deliberate long-term arrangement for companies that need C-level revenue leadership but cannot yet justify a three-hundred-thousand-dollar-plus full-time salary plus equity. They usually serve two to four clients at once, which is why their pattern-matching across companies is often their single most valuable asset.

The sourcing channel matters because a fractional CRO is not a commodity role. You are buying judgment, a network, and a repeatable playbook — none of which show up cleanly on a résumé. A marketplace that specializes in fractional revenue leaders will have already verified that a candidate has actually carried a number as a VP or CRO, has built a sales team from scratch versus merely inheriting one, and understands the difference between founder-led selling and a scalable motion. A generic freelance platform will not. The channel is effectively your first filter, and a weak filter forces you to do all the screening yourself, which is precisely the expertise you are hiring for in the first place. For a deeper primer on when the role makes sense at all, see the fractional leadership overview at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-cro-basics.

There is also a trust dimension. Fractional executives live and die by reputation, so the best ones rarely advertise on open job boards — they get pulled from client to client through referral. This is why the "best place" is frequently not a place at all but a person: an investor, a fellow founder, or a fractional CFO who already works with your company and knows a revenue counterpart. Understanding that dynamic reframes the whole search from "post and pray" to "activate the right network."

## Where are the actual channels to hire a fractional CRO, ranked?

There are six credible channels, and they trade off along two axes: how pre-vetted the candidates are, and how much you pay for that vetting. Warm referrals sit at the top for quality but depend entirely on your network's density. Specialist firms and marketplaces sit in the middle, offering curated candidates for a fee or margin. Open platforms and job boards sit at the bottom for vetting but cost the least and give you the widest raw pool.

The specialist-firm tier is where most well-funded companies land. **Chief Outsiders** is one of the oldest fractional-executive firms and fields fractional CMOs and CROs with enterprise operating backgrounds. **Bespoke Partners** and **Continuum** focus on private-equity-backed and growth-stage companies and are strong when your board wants a known quantity. Newer marketplaces like **Go Fractional**, **Fractional Officer**, and **Bolster** curate independent operators and move faster and cheaper than a retained search. For RevOps-heavy needs specifically, a boutique that lives in the revenue-operations world will understand the difference between a CRO who can inspire a sales floor and one who can architect a CRM and forecasting system — a distinction covered in depth at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-revops-vs-sales-leadership.

Below the firms sit the self-serve options. **LinkedIn** — searching for people whose headline literally reads "Fractional CRO" and who post about go-to-market — is genuinely effective and free, but you own all the vetting. Founder and operator communities (**Pavilion**, **RevGenius**, **On Deck**, **Chief** for women executives) are gold mines because members are pre-selected for seniority and you can ask for references in the same channel. Finally, generalist freelance and consulting platforms (**Toptal**, **Catalant**, **Graphite**) will surface candidates but skew toward project consultants rather than embedded revenue owners, so screen hard for people who have actually owned a quota, not just advised on one.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Need a fractional CRO] --> B{Do you have a strong network}
    B -->|Yes| C[Ask investors and peer CEOs first]
    B -->|No| D{Budget for a firm fee}
    C --> E[Warm referral candidates]
    D -->|Yes| F[Specialist firm or marketplace]
    D -->|No| G[LinkedIn plus operator communities]
    E --> H[Vet and scope engagement]
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I[Trial engagement then ongoing]
```

The practical takeaway: run channels in parallel, not in sequence. Fire off referral requests the same day you brief a specialist firm and start a LinkedIn search. Referrals are highest quality but slowest and least predictable; firms are fastest to a shortlist; self-serve is cheapest but most labor-intensive. Running all three at once compresses a search that would otherwise drag from two months to two weeks.

## How much should a fractional CRO cost, and how is the engagement priced?

Pricing for a fractional CRO clusters into three models: a monthly retainer, a day-rate, or a hybrid of a smaller retainer plus performance upside. Monthly retainers in the current market typically run from around eight thousand to twenty-five thousand dollars per month depending on the company's size, the number of days per week, and the seniority of the operator. Day-rates for the most experienced revenue leaders often land in the fifteen-hundred to three-thousand-dollar range, which is how many independents prefer to price because it protects them from scope creep. The exact number always depends on stage, complexity, and how many days a week you need — never treat any single figure as a fixed market rate.

The channel you choose changes the price. A retained specialist firm adds a margin — often twenty to forty percent on top of the operator's rate — in exchange for vetting, matching, and a replacement guarantee if the fit fails. A marketplace usually takes a thinner platform fee. A direct referral or LinkedIn hire has no intermediary margin at all, so you pay the operator's raw rate, which is why founders with strong networks can get the same caliber of person for meaningfully less. The trade-off is that you also absorb the vetting risk yourself and have no built-in replacement clause.

Beyond the headline rate, structure the engagement to protect both sides. Fractional CROs generally want a minimum commitment — often three to six months — because revenue results take at least a quarter to show, and any operator who promises a turnaround in thirty days is selling hope. A sensible structure is a one-month paid trial or "diagnostic" sprint, where the CRO audits your funnel, forecasting, comp plan, and team, and delivers a written revenue plan. If that plan is sharp, you convert to an ongoing retainer; if it is generic, you have spent one month's fee to learn the fit was wrong. For a full breakdown of comp structures including equity for fractional executives, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-exec-compensation.

## How do you vet a fractional CRO candidate once you have found one?

Vetting a fractional CRO is different from vetting a full-time hire because you are evaluating a portfolio operator, not a single-company careerist. Start with the numbers they have actually owned. Ask for two specific companies where they carried a revenue target, what the starting and ending run-rates were, and what they personally changed — the pricing, the comp plan, the ICP definition, the sales process — to move it. Vague answers about "driving alignment" or "building culture" without a mechanism behind them are the clearest red flag. A real revenue operator talks in funnels, conversion rates, sales-cycle length, and net revenue retention, not adjectives.

Then test for fit with your specific gap. A fractional CRO who scaled a product-led SaaS company from one to ten million is not automatically the right person for an outbound-heavy services business at the same stage — the motions are entirely different. Be explicit about whether your bottleneck is top-of-funnel demand, mid-funnel conversion, sales-team performance, or forecasting and operations, and hire the pattern-match, not the pedigree. The best fractional hires are almost boringly specific: "I fix broken outbound motions for Series A B2B software companies" beats "I do revenue" every time.

Finally, run references sideways, not just down. Anyone will hand you three glowing referees; the signal is in the second-degree check. Ask the referee who else worked with this person, and ask your investor or a community peer what they have heard. Because fractional operators recur through the same networks, reputation travels fast, and a two-minute back-channel often reveals more than a scheduled reference call.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Candidate found] --> B[Ask for two owned revenue numbers]
    B --> C{Concrete mechanisms given}
    C -->|No| D[Reject vague operator]
    C -->|Yes| E[Match motion to your gap]
    E --> F{Motion fits your bottleneck}
    F -->|No| D
    F -->|Yes| G[Back channel references]
    G --> H[Paid diagnostic sprint]
    H --> I[Convert to retainer]
```

One more vetting layer that founders skip: check that the person can actually operate at your altitude. A CRO who has only run three-hundred-person revenue orgs may be miserable and ineffective in a ten-person startup where they need to write the sequences themselves. Ask directly how hands-on they are willing to be, and whether they build the machine or just direct it. For early-stage companies, you almost always want a builder who will get into the CRM, not a delegator who needs a team beneath them to be effective.

## When should you hire a fractional CRO versus a full-time one or a VP of Sales?

The fractional route is right when you have a clear revenue-leadership gap but not enough scale to justify — or afford — a full-time C-level hire. Concretely, that usually means you are between roughly one and fifteen million in revenue, your founder-led sales motion is running out of runway, and you need someone to architect a repeatable go-to-market system before you pour money into headcount. Hiring a two-hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar full-time CRO at that stage is often premature; you would be paying for capacity you cannot yet use.

Conversely, hire full-time when revenue leadership is the single most important job in the company for the next two years — when you are scaling a large sales org, raising a growth round where investors expect a permanent CRO, or when the role requires daily presence that no two-day-a-week arrangement can cover. And consider a VP of Sales instead of any CRO when your gap is narrowly about running and coaching a sales team, not about owning the entire cross-functional revenue engine. A CRO owns marketing alignment, RevOps, and success; a VP of Sales owns the floor. Confusing the two is one of the most expensive hiring mistakes early companies make, explored further at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-cro-vs-vp-sales.

A useful test: if you can write down the specific system you need built — a forecasting model, a comp redesign, an outbound motion, a channel strategy — and it is a finite project with a beginning and end, a fractional CRO or even a project consultant fits. If instead you need a permanent member of the leadership team whose full attention the mission demands, that is a full-time seat. Many companies use the fractional arrangement precisely as a bridge: bring in a fractional CRO to build the machine and define the role, then hire a full-time leader into the seat the fractional executive has already scoped, sometimes with the fractional operator helping run the search.

## What are the common mistakes when hiring a fractional CRO?

The most common mistake is hiring for prestige instead of fit. A logo-heavy résumé from a company ten times your size is seductive, but enterprise revenue leaders often cannot function without the resources, brand, and team they are used to. The right fractional CRO has usually operated at or near your stage recently, remembers what it is like to sell with no brand recognition, and is comfortable being scrappy. Chasing the biggest name is how founders end up paying a premium for advice that does not translate.

The second mistake is fuzzy scoping. Because a fractional CRO is part-time, ambiguity about what they own is corrosive: the CRO thinks they are setting strategy, the founder expected them to close deals, and three months later nothing has moved. Write down, before the engagement starts, exactly what outcomes the CRO is accountable for, what decisions they can make without you, and how many days a week they will actually be present. The tighter the scope, the faster the value. Pair that with a real onboarding — access to your CRM, your data, your team, and your last two quarters of pipeline history — because a fractional hire who spends their first month just getting access is a month of retainer wasted.

The third mistake is treating the search as one-and-done and skipping the trial. The paid diagnostic sprint exists precisely because fractional relationships are cheap to start and expensive to unwind emotionally once your team has bonded with the person. A structured one-month trial with a concrete deliverable de-risks the whole arrangement and gives both sides a clean off-ramp. Founders who skip it to "save time" almost always spend more time later disentangling a bad fit. For a broader checklist on structuring go-to-market leadership hires, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-gtm-leadership-hiring.

## Related questions

### How long does it take to hire a fractional CRO?
Through a specialist firm or marketplace you can have a shortlist in one to two weeks and start within a month. Warm referrals can be faster if the person is available, or slower if they are booked.

### Can a startup with under one million in revenue afford a fractional CRO?
Sometimes, but often a fractional VP of Sales or an advisory arrangement is a better fit at that stage. Below roughly one million, founder-led selling plus targeted RevOps help usually beats a full CRO retainer.

### Do fractional CROs work with competitors at the same time?
Reputable ones avoid direct competitors and will disclose conflicts up front. Always ask about their current client roster and put a non-compete or conflict clause in the agreement.

### Should the fractional CRO help hire their full-time replacement?
Yes, this is a common and healthy pattern. A fractional CRO who has scoped the role and built the machine is well positioned to define the job spec and vet full-time candidates.

### What is the difference between a fractional and an interim CRO?
Interim is full-time and temporary, covering a sudden gap until a permanent hire lands. Fractional is part-time and ongoing, a deliberate long-term arrangement for companies not ready for a full-time seat.

## FAQ

**What is the single best place to start a fractional CRO search?**
Start with warm referrals from your investors and peer CEOs the same day you brief one specialist firm. Referrals give the highest-quality candidates, and the firm guarantees you a shortlist even if referrals come up empty.

**How much does a fractional CRO cost per month?**
Retainers commonly range from roughly eight thousand to twenty-five thousand dollars per month depending on days per week, company complexity, and operator seniority. Day-rates for top operators often fall between fifteen hundred and three thousand dollars. Treat these as ranges, not fixed prices.

**How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?**
Typically one to three days per week, serving two to four clients total. The exact cadence should match your bottleneck — more days early when building the system, fewer once it is running.

**Do I need a specialist firm or can I hire directly?**
You can hire directly through LinkedIn or operator communities and save the firm margin, but you absorb all the vetting and have no replacement guarantee. Firms cost more and move faster with pre-screened candidates and a safety net.

**What should a fractional CRO deliver in the first month?**
A written revenue diagnostic: an audit of your funnel, forecasting, comp plan, ICP, and team, plus a prioritized plan of what to fix first. Use this as a paid trial before committing to an ongoing retainer.

**How do I know if I need a CRO or just a VP of Sales?**
If your gap is running and coaching a sales team, hire a VP of Sales. If you need someone to own the entire cross-functional revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and success — hire a CRO. Do not pay CRO rates for a VP-of-Sales problem.

**Can a fractional CRO convert to full-time later?**
Frequently, yes. Many engagements are designed as a bridge, and a strong fractional operator sometimes takes the permanent seat or helps you hire into it once the company scales enough to justify a full-time leader.

**What red flags should I watch for during vetting?**
Vague answers about "alignment" and "culture" with no mechanism behind them, an inability to cite specific revenue numbers they owned, resistance to a paid trial, and a track record only at companies ten times your size where they relied on resources you do not have.
